name: Dark Plumbeous
lede: Dark Plumbeous is a grayish green from Ridgway's 1912 dictionary, its name Latin for lead-colored, and it shares its exact hex with another of our names, Slate grey.

sections.title: Lead-colored, by name
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 dictionary lists Dark Plumbeous at #5E6A6C, plate LII, hue 49″″″, tone i, and the ISCC-NBS circular of 1955 files it as "dark bluish gray" [1]. *Plumbeous* comes from the Latin *plumbum*, lead, a straightforward description of the dull gray-green of unpolished lead, so unlike most names, the etymology here is plain rather than undocumented [1].

In our color graph the exact same hex is also cataloged under [[slate-grey|Slate grey]], a reminder that two names can describe one identical swatch [1]. The nearest distinct neighbor is [[deep-payne-s-grey|Deep Payne's Grey]], 3.1 units away [1]. The Munsell notation is N 4.3, a neutral value with no hue direction, and the swatch sits with our [[green|green]] family by ISCC convention, close enough to its gray base to also sit near [[grey|grey]] [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this color in 2.04% of 23,781 paintings, 485 of them, as photographed, with the within-painting lens counting 182 [2]. That makes it more common than 69% of our named colors [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 1.5% of the 1,674 paintings from that century, 1.9 times the rate its museums would predict [2]. Within a painting it most often sits as a mid-tone, in 32% of its 182 appearances [2]. John Singer Sargent painted it most often among the artists here, 5 of his 287 works, though no painter stands out against the museum baseline [2]. It is most over-represented in India, 2.3 times the expected rate [2]. It shares canvases with [[greenish-umber|Greenish umber]] more often than chance, at 1.8 times the expected rate [2]. The earliest match dates to 1100, 812 years before Ridgway recorded the name, a floor rather than a first [2].
